summary.text: Writing the rank as \(n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\), harmonic–log bounds together with \(e^{H_{n+1}}=e^{H_n}e^{1/(n+1)}\) and a rational Padé bound for the exponential show \(1\le e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\), so the floor rises by one or two and each rank gap is 2 or 3. Telescoping the two gap counts and using \(e^{H_n}/n\to e^\gamma\) gives the limiting ratio \((e^\gamma-1)/(2-e^\gamma)\); explicit harmonic/log and exponential estimates yield \(16/9<e^\gamma<41/23\), placing it strictly between 3.5 and 3.6.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j
\qquad(n\geq 1),
\]
and put
\[
E_n=e^{H_n}.
\]
We first express the rank sequence in terms of \(E_n\). Since the exponential function is strictly increasing,
\[
\log(k+1)<H_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k+1<E_n.
\]
Thus the number of logarithmic terms \(\log(k+1)\), \(k\geq1\), which occur before \(H_n\) is
\[
\lfloor E_n-1\rfloor.
\]
Consequently the rank of \(H_n\), after also counting the \(n\) harmonic sums \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\), is
\[
a(n)=n+\lfloor E_n-1\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
For completeness, there is no tie between a positive harmonic sum and one of the logarithms: \(H_n\) is a nonzero rational number, whereas an equality \(H_n=\log m\), with integer \(m\geq2\), would say that \(e^{H_n}=m\), contrary to the classical fact that the exponential of a nonzero algebraic number is transcendental. Hence the strict-order count above is indeed the rank in the jointly ordered set. Also \(E_n\geq1\), so the floor in (1) is nonnegative.

We will prove that, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
1\leq E_{n+1}-E_n<2. \tag{2}
\]
Once (2) is known, the assertion about successive differences follows quickly. Most of the work is therefore devoted to (2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Auxiliary logarithmic and exponential inequalities
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We need two elementary estimates for the logarithm. If \(y\geq1\), then
\[
\log y\leq \frac y2-\frac1{2y}. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, define
\[
f(y)=\frac y2-\frac1{2y}-\log y.
\]
For \(y>0\),
\[
f'(y)=\frac{(y-1)^2}{2y^2}\geq0.
\]
Since \(f(1)=0\), (3) follows.

Likewise, for \(y\geq1\),
\[
\frac{2(y-1)}{y+1}\leq\log y. \tag{4}
\]
For
\[
g(y)=\log y-\frac{2(y-1)}{y+1}
\]
one has
\[
g'(y)=\frac{(y-1)^2}{y(y+1)^2}\geq0
\]
when \(y>0\), and again \(g(1)=0\).

We shall also use the following Padé-type upper bound:
\[
e^t(2-t)\leq2+t\qquad(t\geq0). \tag{5}
\]
Here is a direct proof. First set
\[
\psi(t)=1-(1-t)e^t.
\]
Then \(\psi(0)=0\) and
\[
\psi'(t)=te^t\geq0
\]
for \(t\geq0\), so \(\psi(t)\geq0\). Now set
\[
q(t)=2+t-(2-t)e^t.
\]
We have \(q(0)=0\) and
\[
q'(t)=1-(1-t)e^t=\psi(t)\geq0.
\]
Thus \(q(t)\geq0\), which is exactly (5). In particular, whenever \(0\leq t<2\),
\[
e^t\leq\frac{2+t}{2-t}. \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Bounds involving the Euler–Mascheroni constant
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(\gamma\) denote the Euler–Mascheroni constant,
\[
\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}(H_n-\log n).
\]
We first record the standard sharp-sided estimates
\[
H_n-\log(n+1)<\gamma<H_n-\log n \qquad(n\geq1). \tag{7}
\]
They follow, for example, by observing that \(H_n-\log(n+1)\) increases, \(H_n-\log n\) decreases, their difference tends to zero, and both therefore converge to \(\gamma\). Exponentiating (7) gives
\[
e^\gamma n<E_n<e^\gamma(n+1) \qquad(n\geq1). \tag{8}
\]

We will require explicit bounds on \(\gamma\). Introduce
\[
C_n=H_n-\log n-\frac1{2n},
\qquad
D_n=H_n-\log\left(n+\frac12\right).
\]
We claim that \(C_n\) is increasing and \(D_n\) is decreasing.

For \(C_n\), apply (3) to \(y=(n+1)/n\). Since
\[
\log\frac{n+1}{n}=\log(n+1)-\log n,
\]
we obtain
\[
\log(n+1)-\log n
 \leq \frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}
 =\frac1{2n}+\frac1{2(n+1)}.
\]
Using \(H_{n+1}=H_n+1/(n+1)\), rearrangement gives
\[
C_n\leq C_{n+1}. \tag{9}
\]

For \(D_n\), apply (4) to
\[
y=\frac{n+\frac32}{n+\frac12}.
\]
The left side of (4) simplifies to \(1/(n+1)\), and hence
\[
\frac1{n+1}
 \leq \log\left(n+\frac32\right)-\log\left(n+\frac12\right).
\]
Together with \(H_{n+1}=H_n+1/(n+1)\), this gives
\[
D_{n+1}\leq D_n. \tag{10}
\]

Both sequences tend to \(\gamma\). For \(C_n\), this follows from
\[
H_n-\log n\longrightarrow\gamma,
\qquad \frac1{2n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For \(D_n\), write
\[
D_n=(H_n-\log n)-\left(\log\left(n+\frac12\right)-\log n\right).
\]
The second parenthesis is
\[
\log\left(1+\frac1{2n}\right)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore monotonicity and convergence imply
\[
C_{12}\leq\gamma\leq D_{12}. \tag{11}
\]

We now make (11) numerical. Direct summation gives
\[
H_{12}=\frac{86021}{27720}. \tag{12}
\]
The logarithmic estimates needed below are
\[
\log2<0.6931471808,\qquad
\log3\leq1.0987,\qquad
\log5\geq1.6093. \tag{13}
\]
These can all be obtained by rational finite sums from
\[
\frac12\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2j+1}}{2j+1},
 \qquad 0\leq x<1. \tag{14}
\]
More explicitly, its first \(r\) terms give the lower bound
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{x^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
\leq \frac12\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}, \tag{15}
\]
and the omitted tail is at most
\[
\frac{x^{2r+1}}{1-x^2}. \tag{16}
\]
Taking \(x=1/3,r=10\) in the upper estimate gives
\[
\log2\leq
2\left(\sum_{j=0}^{9}\frac{(1/3)^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
+\frac{(1/3)^{21}}{1-1/9}\right)
<0.6931471808.
\]
Taking \(x=1/2,r=7\) in the upper estimate gives \(\log3\leq1.0987\), and taking \(x=2/3,r=10\) in the lower estimate gives \(\log5\geq1.6093\). All the final comparisons here are comparisons of rational numbers.

Since \(12=2^2\cdot3\),
\[
\log12=2\log2+\log3.
\]
Using (11)–(13),
\[
\gamma\geq C_{12}
 =\frac{86021}{27720}-2\log2-\log3-\frac1{24}
 >0.5762. \tag{17}
\]
Indeed, replacing \(\log2\) and \(\log3\) by the upper bounds in (13) gives approximately \(0.57654965\), which is strictly larger than \(0.5762\); the exact comparison is rational.

Also \(12+\tfrac12=25/2\), so
\[
\log\left(12+\frac12\right)=2\log5-\log2.
\]
Hence
\[
\gamma\leq D_{12}
 =\frac{86021}{27720}-2\log5+\log2
 <0.5778. \tag{18}
\]
After inserting (13), the right side is approximately \(0.57775786<0.5778\).

We need two kinds of bounds for \(e^\gamma\). First, since the standard elementary bound \(\gamma>1/2\) holds and \(e^x\geq1+x\),
\[
e^\gamma>e^{1/2}\geq1+\frac12=\frac32. \tag{19}
\]
On the other hand, (5), (18), and positivity of \(2-\gamma\) give
\[
e^\gamma\leq\frac{2+\gamma}{2-\gamma}
 <\frac{181255}{100000}=1.81255. \tag{20}
\]
The last inequality is a direct rational consequence of \(\gamma<5778/10000\).

For the eventual limiting ratio we need slightly different rational bounds:
\[
\frac{16}{9}<e^\gamma<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{21}
\]
To prove the lower bound, (17) and monotonicity of the exponential reduce it to
\[
\frac{16}{9}<e^{5762/10000}.
\]
For every \(x\geq0\), the exponential series gives
\[
e^x\geq\sum_{j=0}^{5}\frac{x^j}{j!}.
\]
At \(x=5762/10000\), direct rational arithmetic yields
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{5}\frac{x^j}{j!}>\frac{16}{9}.
\]
This proves the first half of (21).

For the upper bound, use the elementary remainder estimate valid for \(0\leq x\leq1\):
\[
e^x\leq \sum_{j=0}^{5}\frac{x^j}{j!}
 +\frac{x^6\cdot7}{6!\cdot6}. \tag{22}
\]
This follows by bounding the tail of the exponential series geometrically after the sixth term. At \(x=5778/10000\), a rational calculation gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{5}\frac{x^j}{j!}
 +\frac{x^6\cdot7}{6!\cdot6}<\frac{41}{23}.
\]
Combining this with (18) proves the upper half of (21).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The increment of \(E_n\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Since \(H_{n+1}=H_n+1/(n+1)\),
\[
E_{n+1}=E_n e^{1/(n+1)}. \tag{23}
\]
We need simple global bounds for \(E_n\):
\[
n+1\leq E_n<2n+1\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{24}
\]

For the lower bound, when \(n\geq2\), (8) and (19) give
\[
E_n>e^\gamma n>\frac32n\geq n+1.
\]
When \(n=1\), \(E_1=e>2\), so the same conclusion holds.

For the upper bound, if \(n\geq5\), (8) and (20) give
\[
E_n<1.81255(n+1)\leq2n+1;
\]
the last inequality is immediate for \(n\geq5\). It remains only to check \(n=1,2,3,4\). Here
\[
H_1=1,
\quad H_2=\frac32,
\quad H_3=\frac{11}{6},
\quad H_4=\frac{25}{12}.
\]
Thus it is enough to check
\[
e<3,
\quad e^{3/2}<5,
\quad e^{11/6}<7,
\quad e^{25/12}<9. \tag{25}
\]
These are elementary exponential-series estimates. One convenient common check is first to bound \(e<11/4\) by summing the initial terms of \(\sum1/j!\) and bounding its positive tail. Then
\[
(e^{3/2})^2=e^3<(11/4)^3<5^2,
\]
\[
(e^{11/6})^6=e^{11}<(11/4)^{11}<7^6,
\]
and
\[
(e^{25/12})^{12}=e^{25}<(11/4)^{25}<9^{12};
\]
the power comparisons are rational. Also \(e<3\) directly. Since all quantities are positive, taking the indicated roots proves (25), and hence (24).

We can now prove (2). Put
\[
t=\frac1{n+1}.
\]
From \(e^t\geq1+t\), equations (23) and (24) give
\[
E_{n+1}-E_n=E_n(e^t-1)
 \geq E_n t
 \geq(n+1)\frac1{n+1}=1. \tag{26}
\]

For the upper bound, apply (6) to \(t=1/(n+1)\). A simplification gives
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}
 \leq\frac{2n+3}{2n+1},
\]
and consequently
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}-1\leq\frac2{2n+1}. \tag{27}
\]
Using (23), (24), and (27),
\[
E_{n+1}-E_n
 =E_n\left(e^{1/(n+1)}-1\right)
 \leq E_n\frac2{2n+1}<2. \tag{28}
\]
Together, (26) and (28) establish (2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The successive differences are 2 or 3
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We use the following elementary floor observation. If real numbers \(a,b\) satisfy
\[
1\leq b-a<2,
\]
then
\[
\lfloor b\rfloor-\lfloor a\rfloor\in\{1,2\}. \tag{29}
\]
Indeed, \(b\geq a+1\geq\lfloor a\rfloor+1\), so
\(\lfloor b\rfloor\geq\lfloor a\rfloor+1\). On the other hand,
\(a<\lfloor a\rfloor+1\), and hence
\[
b<a+2<\lfloor a\rfloor+3,
\]
so \(\lfloor b\rfloor<\lfloor a\rfloor+3\). The difference of the two integer floors is therefore either \(1\) or \(2\).

Apply (29) to
\[
a=E_n-1,
\qquad b=E_{n+1}-1.
\]
Condition (2) gives
\[
\lfloor E_{n+1}-1\rfloor-\lfloor E_n-1\rfloor\in\{1,2\}.
\]
Using the rank formula (1),
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)
 =1+\lfloor E_{n+1}-1\rfloor-\lfloor E_n-1\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{2,3\}
\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{30}
\]
This proves the first assertion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Counting the 2s and 3s and taking the limit
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(c_3(N)\) and \(c_2(N)\) be, respectively, the numbers of 3s and 2s among
\[
a(2)-a(1),\ a(3)-a(2),\ldots,\ a(N+1)-a(N).
\]
By (30), every one of these \(N\) differences is exactly one of 2 and 3, so
\[
c_2(N)+c_3(N)=N. \tag{31}
\]
Also \(a(1)=2\): indeed, \(H_1=1\), and \(2<e<3\), so
\[
a(1)=1+\lfloor e-1\rfloor=2.
\]
Telescoping the first \(N\) differences therefore yields
\[
2c_2(N)+3c_3(N)
 =a(N+1)-a(1)=a(N+1)-2. \tag{32}
\]
Solving (31) and (32), we find
\[
c_3(N)=a(N+1)-2-2N, \tag{33}
\]
\[
c_2(N)=3N-(a(N+1)-2). \tag{34}
\]

It remains to determine the first-order growth of \(a(N+1)\). From (1),
\[
a(N+1)=N+1+\lfloor E_{N+1}-1\rfloor. \tag{35}
\]
Now
\[
\frac{E_{N+1}}{N+1}
 =\exp\bigl(H_{N+1}-\log(N+1)\bigr)
 \longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{36}
\]
Since \((N+1)/N\to1\), it follows that
\[
\frac{E_{N+1}}N\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{37}
\]
The floor differs from its argument by less than one. More specifically,
\[
E_{N+1}-2<\lfloor E_{N+1}-1\rfloor\leq E_{N+1}-1,
\]
so
\[
\left|\lfloor E_{N+1}-1\rfloor-E_{N+1}\right|\leq2.
\]
After division by \(N\), this bounded error tends to zero. Hence
\[
\frac{\lfloor E_{N+1}-1\rfloor}{N}\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{38}
\]
Dividing (35) by \(N\), and using \((N+1)/N\to1\), gives
\[
\frac{a(N+1)}N\longrightarrow1+e^\gamma. \tag{39}
\]

Write
\[
G=e^\gamma.
\]
Dividing (33) and (34) by \(N\), then applying (39), gives
\[
\frac{c_3(N)}N
 =\frac{a(N+1)}N-\frac2N-2
 \longrightarrow G-1, \tag{40}
\]
while
\[
\frac{c_2(N)}N
 =3-\frac{a(N+1)}N+\frac2N
 \longrightarrow2-G. \tag{41}
\]
By (21), \(G<41/23<2\), so \(2-G>0\). In particular, \(c_2(N)/N\), and hence \(c_2(N)\), is positive for all sufficiently large \(N\). We may therefore divide (40) by (41) and obtain
\[
\frac{c_3(N)}{c_2(N)}
\longrightarrow L:=\frac{G-1}{2-G}
 =\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}. \tag{42}
\]

Finally, the bounds in (21) locate this limit. Since \(2-G>0\),
\[
L>\frac72
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2(G-1)>7(2-G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
9G>16,
\]
which follows from \(G>16/9\). Similarly,
\[
L<\frac{18}{5}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
5(G-1)<18(2-G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
23G<41,
\]
which follows from \(G<41/23\). Therefore
\[
3.5<L<3.6.
\]

Thus every successive difference \(a(n+1)-a(n)\) is either \(2\) or \(3\), and the ratio of the number of 3s to the number of 2s among the first \(N\) differences tends to
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}},
\]
a number strictly between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\).
